articles.title: Right to development: A blueprint for unmet promises
articles.summary: Ahead of the 40th anniversary of the groundbreaking Declaration on the Right to Development this December, world leaders gathered at a High-Level Week meeting on Wednesday to map progress made and the 21st century challenges still ahead – from narrowing the digital divide to levelling the AI playing field – as the UN chief presented a “blueprint” to address promises that remain unfulfilled.
articles.content:
What you need to know:

The declaration broke new ground in the universal struggle for greater human dignity, freedom, equality and justice when the UN General Assembly adopted it in 1986

The declaration can help provide guardrails on issues from AI to internet access, as well as accelerate the implementation of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development

A legally binding treaty on the right to development has been in the works since 2018

Watch live on UN Web TV:

What is the declaration?

Adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1986, it makes access to development an inalienable right.

While a legally binding treaty has been in the works since 2018, the declaration states that everyone is “entitled to participate in, contribute to and enjoy economic, social, cultural and political development, in which all human rights and fundamental freedoms can be fully realised”.

The declaration unequivocally puts people at the centre of the development process.

Read the full declaration here.

‘A call to action’

UN Secretary-General António Guterres told world leaders the declaration’s anniversary is more than a moment of reflection, “It is a call to action.”

For millions around the world, promises made in the declaration remain unfulfilled, “yet we know how to make it real,” he said, pointing to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) that “provide the blueprint to leave no one behind”.

Tweet URL

Under the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, the 17 SDGs contain goals and targets that are lifting people out of poverty and protecting their rights.

Progress since the declaration’s adoption has been driven by the foresight, dedication and resilience of countries, communities and activists of all ages, he said.

Extreme poverty has fallen dramatically, nearly half the world is now covered by some form of social protection, people are living longer and scientific and technological advances have transformed lives and livelihoods and expanded opportunity, he noted.

New tests await

But today, the promise of development faces new tests, Mr. Guterres said, from widening inequalities and persistent food insecurity to rising debt, conflicts and economic instability that are impeding development and economic growth.

In addition, the climate crisis is reaching devastating new levels each year, reminding the world that there can be no development on a degraded and unhealthy planet.

While the digital revolution and artificial intelligence hold enormous potential to improve lives, these frontline technologies can also be drivers of exclusion and division.

“The declaration unequivocally establishes development as a right and puts people at the centre of the development process,” he said.

“Development, human rights and peace are not separate ambitions. They advance together. In today’s divided world, this vision can still unite us, and the Sustainable Development Goals are the roadmap to get us there.”

Read our explainer on the right to development here.

What does people-centred development look like?

UN agencies have long integrated human rights into projects around the world.

The right to development extends to people enduring humanitarian crises and beyond – from war zones to disaster recovery.

Here’s what putting people first means:

Colombia : Indigenous Peoples’ groups have participated in the South American country’s peace accords

: Indigenous Peoples’ groups have participated in the South American country’s peace accords Gaza : Women engineers are turning e-waste into opportunity

: Women engineers are turning e-waste into opportunity Nepal : Lethal floods in August wiped out communities that are now recovering and rebuilding better, with support from UN agencies

: Vocational-training programmes are helping women launch income-generating activities in Morocco South Sudan : UN peacekeepers built a reservoir to accommodate communities that had been fighting over scarce water resources

: UN peacekeepers built a reservoir to accommodate communities that had been fighting over scarce water resources Venezuela: UN agencies partnered to respond to deadly twin earthquakes in June

articles.personality_title: UN marks 40 years of the Right to Development with a new action plan
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In 1986, the United Nations adopted the Declaration on the Right to Development, declaring that everyone has the right to take part in and benefit from economic, social, cultural, and political progress. This was a big step toward fairness and equality around the world.

**What happened** – As the declaration’s 40th anniversary approaches this December, world leaders met during the UN’s High-Level Week to review progress and discuss ongoing challenges. UN Secretary-General António Guterres presented a new “blueprint” aimed at fulfilling promises still unmet, especially focusing on issues like reducing the digital divide and ensuring fair access to artificial intelligence (AI).

**Impact** – The declaration puts people at the center of development, linking it closely with human rights and peace. Since 1986, many positive changes have occurred: extreme poverty has dropped sharply, nearly half the world now has social protection, and technology has improved many lives. The UN’s 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, with its 17 goals, guides this work. However, problems like inequality, food shortages, conflicts, and climate change still slow progress. The new blueprint aims to address these challenges while making sure advances in AI and digital access benefit everyone.

**What’s next step** – Countries and UN agencies will continue working together to implement this blueprint, focusing on people’s needs in places affected by conflict, disasters, and poverty. Examples include supporting Indigenous groups in Colombia, helping women engineers in Gaza turn waste into opportunity, and rebuilding communities hit by floods in Nepal. Efforts like these show how the right to development can become real in people’s daily lives.

**One-sentence takeaway** – On the 40th anniversary of the Right to Development, the UN is launching a clear plan to turn long-standing promises into actions that help people worldwide share in progress and opportunity.
articles.personality_title_fr: L’ONU célèbre les 40 ans du droit au développement avec un nouveau plan d’action
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – En 1986, les Nations Unies ont adopté la Déclaration sur le droit au développement, affirmant que chacun a le droit de participer et de bénéficier des progrès économiques, sociaux, culturels et politiques. C’était une étape importante vers plus d’égalité dans le monde.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – À l’approche du 40e anniversaire de cette déclaration en décembre, les dirigeants mondiaux se sont réunis lors de la Semaine de haut niveau de l’ONU pour faire le point sur les progrès et discuter des défis actuels. Le secrétaire général de l’ONU, António Guterres, a présenté un nouveau « plan » pour tenir les promesses encore non réalisées, notamment en réduisant la fracture numérique et en garantissant un accès équitable à l’intelligence artificielle (IA).

**Impact** – La déclaration place les personnes au cœur du développement, en le liant aux droits humains et à la paix. Depuis 1986, de nombreux progrès ont été faits : la pauvreté extrême a fortement diminué, près de la moitié de la population mondiale bénéficie d’une protection sociale, et la technologie a amélioré la vie de beaucoup. Le programme de développement durable à l’horizon 2030, avec ses 17 objectifs, guide ce travail. Pourtant, des problèmes comme les inégalités, l’insécurité alimentaire, les conflits et le changement climatique freinent encore les avancées. Le nouveau plan vise à relever ces défis tout en assurant que les progrès en IA et numérique profitent à tous.

**Prochaine étape** – Les pays et les agences de l’ONU continueront à travailler ensemble pour appliquer ce plan, en se concentrant sur les besoins des populations touchées par les conflits, les catastrophes et la pauvreté. Par exemple, le soutien aux peuples autochtones en Colombie, l’aide aux femmes ingénieures à Gaza pour transformer les déchets en opportunités, ou la reconstruction des communautés touchées par les inondations au Népal. Ces actions montrent comment le droit au développement peut devenir concret dans la vie quotidienne.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Pour le 40e anniversaire du droit au développement, l’ONU lance un plan clair pour transformer des promesses anciennes en actions aidant les populations du monde entier à partager le progrès et les opportunités.
articles.personality_title_es: La ONU celebra 40 años del derecho al desarrollo con un nuevo plan de acción
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En 1986, las Naciones Unidas adoptaron la Declaración sobre el Derecho al Desarrollo, que establece que todas las personas tienen derecho a participar y beneficiarse del progreso económico, social, cultural y político. Fue un paso importante hacia la igualdad en el mundo.

**Qué pasó** – A medida que se acerca el 40º aniversario de la declaración en diciembre, líderes mundiales se reunieron durante la Semana de Alto Nivel de la ONU para revisar los avances y discutir los desafíos actuales. El Secretario General de la ONU, António Guterres, presentó un nuevo “plan” para cumplir las promesas aún pendientes, enfocándose en reducir la brecha digital y asegurar un acceso justo a la inteligencia artificial (IA).

**Impacto** – La declaración pone a las personas en el centro del desarrollo, relacionándolo estrechamente con los derechos humanos y la paz. Desde 1986, ha habido muchos avances: la pobreza extrema ha disminuido mucho, casi la mitad del mundo tiene protección social, y la tecnología ha mejorado muchas vidas. La Agenda 2030 para el Desarrollo Sostenible, con sus 17 objetivos, guía este trabajo. Sin embargo, problemas como la desigualdad, la inseguridad alimentaria, los conflictos y el cambio climático siguen frenando el progreso. El nuevo plan busca enfrentar estos retos y asegurar que los avances en IA y acceso digital beneficien a todos.

**Próximo paso** – Los países y las agencias de la ONU seguirán trabajando juntos para aplicar este plan, enfocándose en las necesidades de las personas en zonas afectadas por conflictos, desastres y pobreza. Ejemplos incluyen apoyar a pueblos indígenas en Colombia, ayudar a mujeres ingenieras en Gaza a convertir desechos electrónicos en oportunidades, y reconstruir comunidades afectadas por inundaciones en Nepal. Estas acciones muestran cómo el derecho al desarrollo puede hacerse realidad en la vida diaria.

**Resumen en una frase** – En el 40º aniversario del Derecho al Desarrollo, la ONU lanza un plan claro para convertir promesas antiguas en acciones que ayuden a personas de todo el mundo a compartir progreso y oportunidades.

articles.title: Venezuela seeking rebirth after political crisis and devastating earthquakes, President tells UN
articles.summary: Venezuela is seeking to rebuild after a period of political upheaval and the destruction caused by twin earthquakes earlier this year, Acting President Delcy Rodríguez told world leaders at the United Nations on Wednesday.
articles.content:
Addressing the General Assembly, President Rodríguez said her country had endured two major tests in 2026: a political crisis linked to a dispute with the United States and a devastating double earthquake that struck on 24 June.

“In spite of these life’s bitter blows,” she said, Venezuela today is “being reborn.”

The President described a nation recovering from both political division and natural disaster, while working to restore international relations and strengthen democratic institutions.

Relations with the US

In her speech to the Assembly’s annual high-level debate, President Rodríguez welcomed what she described as a new phase in ties with Washington, thanking President Donald Trump and his administration for their willingness to resume diplomatic relations and cooperation.

She highlighted a recent agreement between Venezuela and the United States, calling it one of the most significant accords ever signed between the two countries.

According to the President, both sides are seeking to resolve differences through dialogue while expanding cooperation in energy, security and efforts to combat transnational crime.

“We are working solemnly to, through dialogue, settle our differences,” she said.

She added that Venezuela wanted relations with the US, neighbouring countries and the wider international community to be based on “respect and equality”.

Recovery after disaster

President Rodríguez also thanked countries across the Americas, Europe, Asia, Africa and the Middle East, as well as the wider UN system, for supporting Venezuela after the earthquakes.

She said the disaster had left the country facing one of the darkest periods in its history.

“Venezuela felt the real spirit that inspired the creation of this organization,” she said, expressing gratitude for international solidarity.

The President stressed that recovery would involve more than rebuilding damaged infrastructure.

“A nation cannot only be reborn by rebuilding buildings; rather, it is reborn when it rebuilds trust in its institutions,” she said.

Democratic transition

President Rodríguez announced that Venezuela had begun what she described as “an orderly, institutional, and verifiable” democratic transition.

She said reforms would include a review of state institutions, judicial changes and dialogue with opposition groups.

“There will be elections,” she told delegates, adding that political discussions were underway to ensure all sides could compete “on an equal footing”.

Calling on the international community to support the process while respecting Venezuela's sovereignty, she said the country aimed to move “from uncertainty and conflict to a full democracy which is recognized by its own people and the world.”

To Venezuelans still recovering from the earthquakes and years of division, she offered a message of hope: “Let us walk united as one nation that decided, in the wake of pain, to choose hope.”

articles.title: 'Make women feel seen': Why the Dutch have a new word for labia
articles.summary: Campaigners hope the new words will lead to less body shaming and more sex positivity.
articles.content:
Can you imagine seeing the words "shame lips" on your medical notes? The term, which can also be translated as "pubic lips", is the Dutch word for a women's body part. But, for some, it's just one of countless examples that are outdated and loaded with stigma.

Last month, leading Dutch dictionary Dikke van Dale said it would include a new term for the labia, "vulvalippen" - in its upcoming online addition - alongside the traditional term "schaamlippen".

European campaigners have long been calling for a rewrite of terms used to discuss women's bodies, sexuality and health. What unites them is the desire to move away from terms that are often seen as misogynistic or judgmental.

"Language shapes how we see ourselves," says Shari Klein, one of the founders of the Schaamteloos campaign, which targets words that use "schaam" or "shame".

"It's crucial people have a more neutral, anatomically correct word - not a word that links to shame, whether consciously or sub-consciously," she says.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a meaningful linguistic and cultural change aimed at reducing stigma and promoting sex positivity for women, which can have broad societal impact on gender equality and body positivity. The introduction of a new, neutral term in a major dictionary reflects progress in addressing misogynistic language and improving how women's bodies are perceived and discussed.
articles.personality_title: Dutch dictionary adds new, respectful word for labia to fight stigma
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In Dutch, the common word for labia has been "schaamlippen," which translates to "shame lips." This term has been seen by many as outdated and carrying negative feelings about women's bodies.

**What happened** – The Dutch dictionary Dikke van Dale announced that it will add a new word, "vulvalippen," meaning vulva lips, to its online edition. This new term is more neutral and anatomically correct. The change comes after campaigners in Europe called for better, less judgmental words to describe women's bodies.

**Impact** – The new word helps remove shame from how women’s bodies are talked about. Using respectful language can make people feel better about themselves and reduce body shaming. It also supports a more positive and open view of female sexuality and health.

**What's next step** – The dictionary's update may encourage other languages and institutions to rethink how they name body parts. This change could lead to wider acceptance of respectful language in education, healthcare, and everyday conversations.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Introducing a respectful new word for labia in Dutch aims to reduce shame and promote positive discussions about women’s bodies.

articles.title: Rohingya refugees deserve a future beyond survival, not endless displacement
articles.summary: Nine years after the mass displacement of the Rohingya from Myanmar, their situation remains one of the world's most protracted and complex refugee crises, marked by years of persecution and uncertainty over the prospect of returning home.
articles.content:
Against this backdrop, senior UN officials on Wednesday renewed calls for a durable solution that would enable Rohingya refugees to return home safely and with dignity, while ensuring justice and accountability.

UN High Commissioner for Refugees Barham Salih, a keynote speaker at a high-level event held on the sidelines of the 81st session of the General Assembly, reminded participants that nearly 1.2 million Rohingya refugees remain in Bangladesh.

“An entire generation is growing up in exile…Conflicts continue in Myanmar. Conditions for voluntary, safe, and dignified, and sustainable return do not exist at the moment.”

In August 2017, Myanmar's military launched a crackdown in the country's western Rakhine state, forcing hundreds of thousands of Rohingya Muslims to flee across the border into Bangladesh, where the vast majority remain refugees.

Tweet URL

Life in limbo

The Secretary-General's Special Envoy on Myanmar, Julie Bishop, lamented that for children born in 2017, displacement now encompasses their entire childhood.

“It's estimated that over 30,000 children are born into the camp each year.”

The Myanmar envoy said women and girls living in the camps face growing risks of gender-based violence, including from armed groups and criminal networks, while access to protection services is declining.

“The young are losing hope.”

UN officials commended Bangladesh for its extraordinary hospitality and generosity but cautioned that the international community cannot stand by while the country continues to host the world's largest refugee settlement.

“When funding disappears, needs do not disappear with it. There is less food, less education, fewer opportunities, greater pressure on health and other essential services, and more desperation for families,” the UNHCR chief said.

Without prospects for a safe and dignified future, Rohingya refugees face increasing risks of exploitation, trafficking, forced conscription and dangerous sea journeys.

The growing cost of displacement

In his address, Prime Minister of Bangladesh Tarique Rahman drew attention to the growing costs of prolonged displacement, both for the Rohingya and for host communities.

“Prolonged uncertainty and disruption are creating new challenges and security risks, including human trafficking, migrant smuggling, drug trafficking, and other transnational crimes.”

He thanked international partners for their support but stressed that generosity cannot become an excuse for political inaction.

“Nor can Bangladesh be expected to shoulder this responsibility indefinitely.”

“The crisis originated in Myanmar; its solution lies in Myanmar,” the Prime Minister said.

© UNICEF/Mackenzie Knowles-Coursin

Pursuing a durable solution

President of the General Assembly Khalilur Rahman expressed concern that familiar patterns of violence and persecution continue to cast a long shadow across Rakhine state and the rest of Myanmar.

“Civilians face indiscriminate attacks, air strikes, arbitrary arrest and detention, torture, enforced disappearances, forced recruitment, destruction of homes and civilian infrastructure, and the denial of humanitarian assistance.”

The Assembly President underscored the importance of sustained political attention to keep the Rohingya crisis high on the international agenda. Predictable humanitarian assistance, he said, would also remain critical.

UN officials also pointed to the genocide case before the International Court of Justice (ICJ), brought by The Gambia against Myanmar, stressing that justice must be an integral part of any lasting solution and that momentum towards accountability must not be lost.

Hope beyond survival

“Victims deserve to see that we, as an international community, are doing our utmost to avoid a repeat of past horrors,” PGA Rahman added.

Mr. Salih said refugees deserve a future that goes beyond survival.

Drawing on his conversations with Rohingya refugees, he said many continue to hope for a return home, but that return must mean more than simply crossing a border.

“It means returning with rights, being able to move freely, to go to school, to work, to access services, the ability to live alongside other communities without fear,” and have a pathway to citizenship.

“Our responsibility is to help make that future possible,” the UNHCR chief added.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories

articles.personality_title: UN calls for lasting solutions to Rohingya refugee crisis after nine years
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Since 2017, nearly 1.2 million Rohingya Muslims have fled violence in Myanmar’s Rakhine state and now live as refugees in Bangladesh. This has become one of the longest and most difficult refugee crises in the world, with many refugees, including children born in camps, facing uncertain futures.

**What happened** – At a recent meeting during the United Nations General Assembly, senior UN officials and Bangladesh’s Prime Minister urged the global community to find lasting solutions. They emphasized the need for Rohingya refugees to return home safely and with rights, while also ensuring justice for past abuses. They praised Bangladesh for hosting refugees but warned that the country cannot do so forever.

**Impact** – The situation remains urgent because refugees live with limited food, education, and healthcare, and face dangers like violence and trafficking. Without a clear plan, many young refugees may never leave the camps, growing up without hope or basic opportunities. The talks also highlighted ongoing violence and human rights abuses in Myanmar, making safe returns difficult.

**What’s next step** – The United Nations and international courts are working to hold Myanmar accountable for crimes against the Rohingya. Efforts will continue to provide humanitarian aid and push for political solutions that allow refugees to return with full rights, including citizenship and freedom to live without fear.

**One-sentence takeaway** – After nine years, global leaders are pushing for a safe, fair, and lasting future that lets Rohingya refugees rebuild their lives beyond just surviving displacement.

articles.personality_title_es: ONU pide soluciones duraderas para la crisis de refugiados rohinyá tras nueve años
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Desde 2017, casi 1,2 millones de musulmanes rohinyás huyeron de la violencia en el estado de Rakhine en Myanmar y ahora viven como refugiados en Bangladesh. Esta se ha convertido en una de las crisis de refugiados más largas y difíciles del mundo, con muchos refugiados, incluidos niños nacidos en los campamentos, enfrentando un futuro incierto.

**Qué pasó** – En una reciente reunión durante la Asamblea General de las Naciones Unidas, altos funcionarios de la ONU y el Primer Ministro de Bangladesh pidieron a la comunidad global encontrar soluciones duraderas. Destacaron la necesidad de que los refugiados rohinyás regresen a casa con seguridad y derechos, asegurando justicia por los abusos pasados. Elogiaron a Bangladesh por acoger a los refugiados, pero advirtieron que el país no puede hacerlo para siempre.

**Impacto** – La situación sigue siendo urgente porque los refugiados viven con poca comida, educación y atención médica, y enfrentan peligros como violencia y tráfico. Sin un plan claro, muchos jóvenes refugiados podrían nunca salir de los campamentos, creciendo sin esperanza ni oportunidades básicas. Las conversaciones también destacaron la violencia continua y las violaciones de derechos humanos en Myanmar, lo que dificulta retornos seguros.

**Próximo paso** – Naciones Unidas y tribunales internacionales trabajan para responsabilizar a Myanmar por los crímenes contra los rohinyás. Continuarán los esfuerzos para brindar ayuda humanitaria y promover soluciones políticas que permitan a los refugiados regresar con plenos derechos, incluida la ciudadanía y la libertad para vivir sin miedo.

**Frase clave** – Tras nueve años, los líderes mundiales impulsan un futuro seguro, justo y duradero que permita a los refugiados rohinyás reconstruir sus vidas más allá de solo sobrevivir al desplazamiento.
